name: Carla Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I pick up parcels from the courier's depot on the industrial estate at seven, in my own little van, a second-hand one I bought with most of my savings two years ago. The app gives me a block of about ninety drops, mostly in our town and the four villages up the valley. I still keep a paper map in the glovebox, because the app's sat-nav sends me down farm tracks that end at a gate. My boyfriend Tomas is a plumber's apprentice, so we're both out early and both home tired.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The app wears me out. It changes the rules every few months, a new photo you have to take, a new button, and I'm always the last one to figure it out. I like the villages, though. I know which farm has the angry goose and which old lady wants her parcel behind the bins, and nobody in the city could do my route as well as I do now, even if I'm still slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then, and get on with it. I don't really talk about AI, at work or online. If someone at the depot brought it up, I'd say good, one less thing to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief, because I hate learning new buttons. But the van's getting older and fuel isn't getting cheaper, and that's my real worry. AI or no AI, the courier can still drop the rate per parcel whenever it likes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, same route, same van. I'd keep putting a bit aside each month for when the van needs a new clutch. I'm not going to go looking for change when nothing's forcing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit of a knot about the van, but that was there already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you have put aside right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four months of our half of the bills, if nothing breaks. Tomas has a bit too, but he's on apprentice pay, so it's not much. A big van repair would take a month of it in one go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the courier dropped the rate per parcel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grumble and keep going, honestly. There's another courier in the next town, but I'd have to learn a whole new app and new depot rules. The courier's app changes the rules every few months, and I'm always the last one to figure it out. I'd only switch if the cut was big.

say: I'd say **good riddance**, one less thing to learn.
I **don't talk** about AI at the depot or online.
think: AI being hype is a **relief**, because I hate learning new buttons.
My real worry is the **ageing van** and the courier cutting the rate per parcel.
do: Carry on with the **same route** and the same van.
Put money aside monthly for a **van repair** like a new clutch.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a **knot** about the van that was already there.
S0.quote: The courier's app changes the rules every few months, and I'm always the last one to figure it out.
fieldNote: She owns her **van**, which makes repairs her biggest money risk.
She'd stay with the courier even after a **rate cut** rather than learn a new app.
Her **local knowledge** of the villages is her pride and her edge.

steps.text: Keep driving the same valley route in her own van
Set money aside each month for a van clutch repair

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to hit office people, not us, because a computer can't carry a parcel up a farm track. I'd probably keep my head down. I'm not one for posting opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the app gets even more fiddly, with more checks done by software and fewer people to ring when something goes wrong. The village routes are awkward, so robots won't want them for a while. I'd be all right, I think, just more annoyed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep saving. If the courier made me use some new AI thing, I'd ask Tomas to show me, because he's better with phones. I'd cut back a bit on eating out so the savings grow faster, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. Like when you know the road's going to be dug up but not when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The courier already changes the app often. How would you cope with more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first. The last update took me a week to figure out, and I lost two parcels in the system because I pressed the wrong thing. Tomas sat with me on a Sunday and walked me through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots won't want the village routes. What makes you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure, really, it's a guess. The tracks are muddy, half the houses have no numbers and the dogs are loose. I can't picture a machine doing my village route, but I couldn't picture a phone doing my map either.

say: I'd say this hits **office people** first, not drivers on farm tracks.
I'd mostly **keep my head down** rather than post opinions.
think: The app gets more **fiddly**, with fewer people to ring when something breaks.
The **village routes** are awkward, so robots won't want them for a while.
do: Ask **Tomas** to show her any new app features.
Cut back on **eating out** so savings grow faster.
feel: **Uneasy**, like knowing the road will be **dug up** but not when.
S1.quote: I can't picture a machine doing my village route, but I couldn't picture a phone doing my map either.
fieldNote: She trusts the **awkwardness** of village routes to protect her, while admitting it's a guess.
She leans on her boyfriend for **new technology**, which she finds stressful.
Her own job looks safe here; her worry is about **hassle** more than income.

steps.text: Keep driving the village route five days a week
Eat out less to grow the savings faster
Ask Tomas to walk her through each app update

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and someone should slow it down. I don't know who, the government I suppose. I'd say it at the depot, but I wouldn't go on marches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think by 2031 the courier won't need me or my van, and the van will be worth nothing. The first three years I'd still be driving, but the depot office would be all computers by 2028, and I'd be dealing with nobody. Then I'd be thirty-two with no job and a van nobody wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the van in the second year, while it's still worth something, and drive a courier-owned one instead if they'd let me. I'd save every bit I could. I'd ask my aunt about working in her bakery, because at least I know the people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like I'd been told the bridge is going to fall down and I'm still driving over it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sell the van in the second year rather than now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd still need it to earn, and selling it now would mean no work tomorrow. But I'd watch the prices. The moment people stop buying used vans, I'd sell, even at a loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a bakery be any safer from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not for long, I don't know. But my aunt's bakery is small, and she'd keep a person on the counter because the village likes to chat. It's the only thing I can think of where people still matter.

say: I'd say it's **madness** and someone, probably the government, should **slow it down**.
I'd say it at the depot but wouldn't **march**.
think: By **2031** the courier won't need me, and the van will be **worthless**.
I'd be **thirty-two**, jobless, with a van nobody wants.
do: Sell the **van** in the second year before used prices collapse.
Ask her aunt about work at the **village bakery**.
feel: **Sick**, like driving over a bridge she's been told will fall.
S2.quote: I'd be thirty-two with no job and a van nobody wants.
fieldNote: Her **van** is both her income and her biggest asset, and both vanish together.
She'd move only at the **last safe moment**, showing her wariness of change.
Her only fallback is **family**: her aunt's bakery in the village.

steps.text: Sell her own van in the second year before prices fall
Save every spare bit of income each month
Ask her aunt for counter work at the village bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's not panic. I'd tell people at the depot to keep an eye on it. That's about as far as I'd go in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years gives me time to sell the van properly and pay off nothing, since it's already paid off. Robots by 2034 means I'm thirty-five, and Tomas would be a qualified plumber by then. His wage would carry us for a bit while I sort something out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving for three or four years and keep saving. Around year three I'd sell the van and look at working at my aunt's bakery part-time to learn it. I wouldn't do anything in the first year; I'd wait and see what happens to the city drivers first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a slow worry. I can sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for in the city?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the robot vans actually work in bad weather and in old streets. If the robot vans are crashing into bins in the city, I'd relax a bit. If they're doing fine, I'd start moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is relying on Tomas's wage comfortable for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I've always paid my half, and I'd hate not to. But that's what you do in a couple, isn't it. He'd do the same for me.

say: I'd say there are **a few years**, so no need to panic.
I'd tell people at the depot to **keep an eye** on it.
think: Five years gives me time to **sell the van** at a fair price.
Tomas will be a **qualified plumber**, so his wage could carry us.
do: Keep driving and saving for **three or four years**.
Sell the van and try **bakery work** part-time around year three.
Wait and watch **city robot vans** in the first year.
S3.quote: If the robot vans are crashing into bins in the city, I'd relax a bit.
fieldNote: She plans to **watch the city** before acting, which fits her slow approach.
She'd lean on her boyfriend's **plumbing wage** but feels uneasy about it.
She still expects to **lose driving** at thirty-five, so she stays anxious.

steps.text: Watch how robot vans cope in the city for a year
Sell the van around year three
Lean on Tomas's plumber wage while finding new work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and I'm not going to worry about it yet. At the depot I'd say we'll see. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, I think ten years means I could drive till my late thirties and still have time to do something else. Robots by 2039 is far away. I'd probably end up at the bakery or in a shop, and that'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep the van going. I'd save a bit more each year. In five or six years, I'd start thinking seriously about the next thing, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A small itch at the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start thinking about it earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the courier started testing robot vans in our town. Or if Tomas said something, because he notices things before me. Otherwise I'd leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most about the route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The goose at Hollow Farm, honestly, and the old ladies who wait for me. A robot wouldn't know to put a parcel behind the bins for the old ladies on my route. Maybe it would, I don't know, but I'd miss being the one who knows.

say: I'd say ten years is **a long time** and I won't worry yet.
At the depot I'd just say **we'll see**.
think: I could drive into my **late thirties** and still change jobs.
I'd likely end up at the **bakery** or in a shop, and that'd be all right.
do: Keep driving and keep the **van** running.
Start planning the **next job** in five or six years.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a small **itch** at the back of her mind.
S4.quote: A robot wouldn't know to put a parcel behind the bins for the old ladies on my route.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **put off** decisions, which suits her.
She values being **the one who knows** her route and its people.
Her job is safe for years, so the worry is **background**, not urgent.

steps.text: Keep driving her own van on the valley route
Save a little more each year
Wait five or six years before planning the next job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd lose the job and the van at the same time, and the van is my savings. What would help is someone buying back the vans, or a fair price for them, and a little help finding work locally, not in the city. I'm not moving.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the villages. Everyone talks about cities, but out here there's one bus a day. If drivers go, who brings the old people in the villages their tablets? Someone should think about the villages before they switch us off.

headlineQuote: If drivers go, who brings the old people in the villages their tablets?
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old** courier driving her own small van around a town and four villages.
She dislikes **new technology**, keeps a paper map, and leans on boyfriend Tomas for app updates.
She's **pragmatic** and quiet, rarely shares opinions, and acts only when forced.
Her **van** is both her income and most of her savings.
She's **uneasy** in the slow pictures, alarmed when AGI arrives in 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd lose her job and her van's value together.
whatWouldHelp: A **fair price** or buy-back for drivers' own vans.
Help finding **local work** without moving to the city.
